claim: Post-translationally modified peptides are involved in many aspects of plant growth and development.
source: Post-translationally modified peptides are involved in many aspects of plant growth and development.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: The biogenesis of CLEL6 and CLEL9 peptides in Arabidopsis thaliana requires a series of processing events in consecutive compartments of the secretory pathway.
source: We show here that the biogenesis of CLEL6 and CLEL9 peptides in Arabidopsis thaliana requires a series of processing events in consecutive compartments of the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript including localization studies and processing assays.

claim: Following cleavage of the signal peptide upon entry into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the peptide precursors are processed in the cis-Golgi by the subtilase SBT6.1.
source: Following cleavage of the signal peptide upon entry into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the peptide precursors are processed in the cis-Golgi by the subtilase SBT6.1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing processing patterns and localization studies with BFA treatment and Golgi markers.

claim: SBT6.1-mediated cleavage within the variable domain allows for continued passage of the partially processed precursors through the secretory pathway.
source: SBT6.1-mediated cleavage within the variable domain allows for continued passage of the partially processed precursors through the secretory pathway, and for subsequent post-translational modifications including tyrosine sulfation and proline hydroxylation within, and proteolytic maturation after exit from the Golgi.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that mutation of SBT6.1 cleavage sites impairs secretion (Figure 2I,F).

claim: Activation by subtilases including SBT3.8 in post-Golgi compartments depends on the N-terminal aspartate of the mature peptides.
source: Activation by subtilases including SBT3.8 in post-Golgi compartments depends on the N-terminal aspartate of the mature peptides.
evidence: This is supported by site-directed mutagenesis experiments showing that D71A and D66A mutations prevent processing (Figure 4A,B).

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, there are more than 1000 genes potentially encoding signaling peptides.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana (hereafter 'Arabidopsis'), there are more than 1000 genes potentially encoding signaling peptides, apparently involved in all aspects of plant growth and development (Lease and Walker, 2006; Ghorbani et al., 2015; Tavormina et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tyrosine sulfation is performed by a single tyrosylprotein sulfotransferase (TPST) that is membrane-anchored in the cis-Golgi.
source: Tyrosine sulfation is performed by a single tyrosylprotein sulfotransferase (TPST) that is membrane-anchored in the cis-Golgi (Komori et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TPST requires aspartate on the amino side of tyrosin for substrate recognition.
source: TPST requires aspartate on the amino side of tyrosin for substrate recognition (Komori et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Tyrosine sulfation is a critical maturation step, as sulfated peptides usually depend on this modification for full activity.
source: Tyrosine sulfation is a critical maturation step, as sulfated peptides usually depend on this modification for full activity (Stührwohldt and Schaller, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Proline hydroxylation is catalyzed by membrane-anchored prolyl-4-hydroxylases (P4Hs) localized in ER and Golgi compartments.
source: Proline hydroxylation is catalyzed by membrane-anchored prolyl-4-hydroxylases (P4Hs) localized in ER and Golgi compartments.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: There are 13 P4Hs in Arabidopsis.
source: There are 13 P4Hs in Arabidopsis, some of which were shown to be required for the hydroxylation of extensin and possibly other hydroxyprolin (Hyp)-rich glycoproteins of the cell wall (Velasquez et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: HPAT is encoded by three genes in Arabidopsis that are at least partially functionally redundant.
source: HPAT is encoded by three genes in Arabidopsis that are at least partially functionally redundant (Ogawa-Ohnishi et al., 2013; MacAlister et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There are 907 peptidases listed in the MEROPS database (release 12.0) for Arabidopsis.
source: It was and is still hampered by the large number of possible candidates (907 peptidases are listed in the MEROPS database (release 12.0) for Arabidopsis Rawlings et al., 2016), by their generally low expression levels, by functional redundancy, and by the lack of a conserved processing site.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the MEROPS database.

claim: There is no consensus motif that would mark the cleavage sites for processing of peptide precursors in plants.
source: As compared to tyrosine sulfation, proline hydroxylation and Hyp arabinosylation which occur at Asp-Tyr, Pro, and Hyp residues, respectively, and in contrast to animal systems, where peptide hormones are typically flanked by pairs of basic residues, there is no consensus motif that would mark the cleavage sites for processing of peptide precursors in plants (Rawlings et al., 2016; Stührwohldt and Schaller, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SBTs constitute a large family of mostly extracellular proteases including 56 members in Arabidopsis.
source: SBTs constitute a large family of mostly extracellular proteases including e.g. 56 members in Arabidopsis (Rautengarten et al., 2005), 86 in tomato (Reichardt et al., 2018) and 97 in grapevine (Figueiredo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AtSBT6.1 is a membrane protein, anchored by a C-terminal membrane-spanning helix to the Golgi and possibly the plasma membrane.
source: First, unlike most other plant SBTs that are soluble proteins targeted to the cell wall (Schaller et al., 2018), AtSBT6.1 is a membrane protein, anchored by a C-terminal membrane-spanning helix to the Golgi and possibly the plasma membrane (Liu et al., 2007a; Ghorbani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AtSBT6.1 is one of only two Arabidopsis SBTs that originated before the divergence of Metazoa and Viridiplantae.
source: Second, AtSBT6.1 is one of only two Arabidopsis SBTs that originated before the divergence of Metazoa and Viridiplantae, and is functionally conserved between animals and plants (Taylor and Qiu, 2017; Schaller et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AtSBT6.1 cleaves membrane-anchored bZIP transcription factors in the Golgi to facilitate the translocation of their cytoplasmic domain to the nucleus for the induction of ER stress-response genes.
source: Like Site-1-Protease (S1P), its orthologue in humans, AtSBT6.1 (alias AtS1P) cleaves membrane-anchored bZIP transcription factors in the Golgi to facilitate the translocation of their cytoplasmic domain to the nucleus for the induction of ER stress-response genes (Liu et al., 2007b; Liu et al., 2007a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The cleavage site preference of AtSBT6.1 is for the amino acid motives R-(R/K)-X-L or R-(R/K)-L-X.
source: Furthermore, the cleavage site preference of AtSBT6.1 for the amino acid motives R-(R/K)-X-L or R-(R/K)-L-X (Srivastava et al., 2009; Ghorbani et al., 2016) is almost identical with the substrate specificity reported for human S1P (R-X-(L/V/I)-X; Seidah, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The substrate specificity of human S1P is R-X-(L/V/I)-X.
source: Furthermore, the cleavage site preference of AtSBT6.1 for the amino acid motives R-(R/K)-X-L or R-(R/K)-L-X (Srivastava et al., 2009; Ghorbani et al., 2016) is almost identical with the substrate specificity reported for human S1P (R-X-(L/V/I)-X; Seidah, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: AtSBT6.1 has predominant Golgi localization.
source: With its predominant Golgi localization (Liu et al., 2007a; Parsons et al., 2012), AtSBT6.1 seems predestined to act in concert with TPST, P4Hs and HPATs in the biogenesis of post-translationally modified signaling peptides.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CLEL family comprises 11 precursor-derived peptides of 13 to 18 amino acids carrying two additional post-translational modifications, i.e. tyrosine sulfation and hydroxylation of the ultimate proline residue.
source: The latter is also known as Golven (GLV) or Root Meristem Growth Factor (RGF) family and comprises 11 precursor-derived peptides of 13 to 18 amino acids carrying two additional post-translational modifications, i.e. tyrosine sulfation and hydroxylation of the ultimate proline residue (Matsuzaki et al., 2010; Meng et al., 2012; Whitford et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AtSBT6.1 was identified as a factor required for CLEL6 function in a screen for sbt mutants suppressing the CLEL6-overexpression phenotype.
source: AtSBT6.1 was identified as a factor required for CLEL6 function in a screen for sbt mutants suppressing the CLEL6-overexpression phenotype (agravitropic root growth and increased hypocotyl elongation) (Ghorbani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: AtSBT6.1 cleaves the CLEL6 precursor at two canonical AtSBT6.1/S1P cleavage sites (R-R-L-R, R-R-A-L).
source: The protease was shown to cleave the CLEL6 precursor at two canonical AtSBT6.1/S1P cleavage sites (R-R-L-R, R-R-A-L), and both cleavage sites turned out to be relevant for CLEL6 function, the second one even essential.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Ghorbani et al., 2016).

claim: Both AtSBT6.1 cleavage sites are relevant for CLEL6 function, the second one even essential.
source: The protease was shown to cleave the CLEL6 precursor at two canonical AtSBT6.1/S1P cleavage sites (R-R-L-R, R-R-A-L), and both cleavage sites turned out to be relevant for CLEL6 function, the second one even essential.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Ghorbani et al., 2016).

claim: Seedlings expressing EPI1a under the control of either the CLEL6 or the CLEL9 promoter were impaired in the gravitropic response of the hypocotyl.
source: Seedlings expressing EPI1a under the control of either the CLEL6 or the CLEL9 promoter were impaired in the gravitropic response of the hypocotyl (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1C.

claim: Hypocotyl gravitropism was inhibited by the expression of EPI10 controlled by either the CLEL6 or CLEL9 promoter.
source: Likewise, hypocotyl gravitropism was inhibited also by the expression of EPI10 controlled by either one of the two CLEL promoters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The gravitropic response of roots was not affected in EPI-expressing transgenics.
source: However, in contrast to CLEL6 or 9-silenced plants (Whitford et al., 2012), the gravitropic response of roots was not affected in our EPI-expressing transgenics (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The CLEL6 and 9 promoters are active in the hypocotyl where they drive the expression of EPI inhibitors in epidermis and cortex.
source: This observation is consistent with the fact that the CLEL6 and 9 promoters are active in the hypocotyl where they drive the expression of EPI inhibitors in epidermis and cortex (Whitford et al., 2012), but not in any part of the primary root (Fernandez et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The CLEL6 and 9 promoters are not active in any part of the primary root.
source: This observation is consistent with the fact that the CLEL6 and 9 promoters are active in the hypocotyl where they drive the expression of EPI inhibitors in epidermis and cortex (Whitford et al., 2012), but not in any part of the primary root (Fernandez et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Gravicurvature of PCLEL6:EPI1a and PCLEL9:EPI1a lines is restored to wild-type levels by application of 10 nM CLEL6 or 300 nM CLEL9.
source: When plants expressing the EPI1a inhibitor were supplied with synthetic CLEL6 or CLEL9 peptides, gravitropism of the hypocotyl was restored to wild-type level (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1D.

claim: tpst-1 mutants have an impaired gravitropic response.
source: Likewise, we observed an impaired gravitropic response in mutants defective in tyrosylprotein sulfotransferase (TPST), and the defect of the tpst-1 mutant also was alleviated by application of the sulfated CLEL6 or CLEL9 peptides (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: The defect of the tpst-1 mutant is alleviated by application of the sulfated CLEL6 or CLEL9 peptides.
source: Likewise, we observed an impaired gravitropic response in mutants defective in tyrosylprotein sulfotransferase (TPST), and the defect of the tpst-1 mutant also was alleviated by application of the sulfated CLEL6 or CLEL9 peptides (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: The peptides act downstream of SBT (and TPST) activity.
source: The data indicate that the peptides act downstream of SBT (and TPST) activity, consistent with a role for SBTs (and TPST) in peptide maturation (Figure 1B,D–F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the complementation experiments showing that exogenous peptides rescue the phenotype.

claim: The CLEL6 precursor comprises two potential S1P (SBT6.1) cleavage sites, RRLR and RRAL.
source: The CLEL6 precursor comprises two potential S1P (SBT6.1) cleavage sites, RRLR and RRAL (Figure 2A), and the second site is necessary for CLEL6 function (Ghorbani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2A and citation to previous work.

claim: The second SBT6.1 cleavage site (RRAL) is necessary for CLEL6 function.
source: The CLEL6 precursor comprises two potential S1P (SBT6.1) cleavage sites, RRLR and RRAL (Figure 2A), and the second site is necessary for CLEL6 function (Ghorbani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GFP fluorescence of the secreted CLEL6 construct (Sec) was detected only in the apoplast.
source: GFP fluorescence was detected only in the apoplast (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: On an anti-GFP immunoblot of the secreted CLEL6 construct, a single band was detected corresponding in size to GFP with part of the precursor up to the first SBT6.1 cleavage site.
source: On an anti-GFP immunoblot a single band was detected corresponding in size to GFP with part of the precursor up to the first SBT6.1 cleavage site (Figure 2E, red asterisk).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Processing at the first SBT6.1 cleavage site is efficient when the precursor is allowed to pass through the secretory pathway.
source: Processing at this site is thus efficient when the precursor is allowed to pass through the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of a single processed band in the secreted construct.

claim: When the CLEL6 precursor was equipped with a C-terminal KDEL-motif for ER retention, processing was incomplete.
source: When the precursor was equipped with a C-terminal KDEL-motif for ER retention (construct named 'KDEL' in Figure 2B), processing was incomplete (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For the KDEL-tagged precursor, the fluorescence signal was detected in the ER, Golgi, and apoplast.
source: In addition to the apoplast, the fluorescence signal was now detected also in the ER and Golgi, as indicated by co-expression of ER (Vma12-mRFP) or Golgi (ManI-mCherry and ST-mCherry for early and late Golgi, respectively) markers (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Processing of the KDEL-tagged CLEL6 precursor was abolished when anterograde ER-to-Golgi vesicle transport was inhibited by addition of brefeldin A.
source: However, processing was abolished when anterograde ER-to-Golgi vesicle transport was inhibited by addition of brefeldin A (Nebenführ et al., 2002; Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C and citation to previous work on BFA.

claim: Exit from the ER is required for cleavage by SBT6.1.
source: These observations indicate that exit from the ER is required for cleavage by SBT6.1, and we conclude that SBT6.1 acts in the Golgi, likely in an early Golgi compartment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the BFA treatment experiment showing no processing when ER exit is blocked.

claim: SBT6.1 acts in the Golgi, likely in an early Golgi compartment.
source: These observations indicate that exit from the ER is required for cleavage by SBT6.1, and we conclude that SBT6.1 acts in the Golgi, likely in an early Golgi compartment.
evidence: This is an inference based on BFA treatment and localization studies with Golgi markers.

claim: Cleavage by SBT6.1 occurs before the precursor reaches the trans Golgi network (TGN).
source: The same three cleavage products were observed as for the KDEL-tagged precursor at somewhat different ratios (Figure 2E) indicating that cleavage by SBT6.1 occurs before the precursor reaches the trans Golgi network (TGN).
evidence: This is an inference based on the processing pattern of the XylT-tagged construct which is retained in the medial Golgi.

claim: Secretion of the Ala-substituted CLEL6 precursor is reduced compared to the wild-type.
source: Interestingly, comparing Figure 2D and I, we observed that secretion of the Ala-substituted precursor is reduced compared to the wild-type.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data comparing Figure 2D and 2I.

claim: Cleavage by SBT6.1 may facilitate continued passage along the secretory pathway.
source: For the Ala-substituted precursor, the GFP fluorescence signal was observed in both ER and Golgi in addition to the apoplastic space suggesting that cleavage by SBT6.1 may facilitate continued passage along the secretory pathway and, hence, additional post-translational modifications in post-Golgi compartments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutation of SBT6.1 sites leads to accumulation in ER and Golgi.

claim: For the Δ-Sec construct, a single band was detected corresponding in size to the precursor processed at the N-terminal maturation site.
source: On an anti-GFP immunoblot a single band was detected for Δ-Sec corresponding in size to the precursor processed at the N-terminal maturation site (Figure 3C, blue asterisk).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For Δ-Sec, some of the GFP signal was observed in the cell wall, in addition to the ER and a weak signal in the late Golgi.
source: Interestingly, for Δ-Sec some of the GFP signal was observed in the cell wall, in addition to the ER and a weak signal in the late Golgi (ST-mCherry marker in Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Secretion of the Δ-Sec construct is reduced compared to wild-type Sec.
source: Secretion of this construct, like that of Secm (Figure 2I), is thus reduced compared to wild-type Sec (Figure 2D), suggesting that the propeptide, in addition to propeptide cleavage by SBT6.1 (Figure 2I), may contribute to efficient passage through the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of fluorescence patterns between different constructs.

claim: The propeptide may contribute to efficient passage through the secretory pathway.
source: Secretion of this construct, like that of Secm (Figure 2I), is thus reduced compared to wild-type Sec (Figure 2D), suggesting that the propeptide, in addition to propeptide cleavage by SBT6.1 (Figure 2I), may contribute to efficient passage through the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that deletion of the propeptide reduces secretion efficiency.

claim: The unprocessed precursors were observed for both Δ-KDEL and Δ-XylT as single larger bands on the immunoblot.
source: In contrast to Δ-Sec, the unprocessed precursors were observed for both Δ-KDEL and Δ-XylT as single larger bands on the immunoblot (Figure 3C, black asterisk).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The GFP signal for the Δ-KDEL construct was found exclusively in the ER.
source: The GFP signal for the C-terminally KDEL-tagged deletion (Δ) construct was found exclusively in the ER (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Retention of the N-terminal GFP tag in the ER confirmed that processing did not occur for Δ-KDEL.
source: Retention of the N-terminal GFP tag in the ER confirmed that processing did not occur, indicating that the maturation step is located further downstream in the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization and processing data.

claim: The maturation step is located further downstream in the secretory pathway than the ER.
source: Retention of the N-terminal GFP tag in the ER confirmed that processing did not occur, indicating that the maturation step is located further downstream in the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ER-retained constructs are not processed.

claim: For Δ-XylT the apparently unprocessed precursor co-localized exclusively with Golgi markers.
source: For Δ-XylT the apparently unprocessed precursor (Figure 3C) co-localized exclusively with Golgi markers (Figure 3F), suggesting a post-Golgi compartment or, at the latest, the apoplastic space as the site for CLEL6 maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A post-Golgi compartment or the apoplastic space is the site for CLEL6 maturation.
source: For Δ-XylT the apparently unprocessed precursor (Figure 3C) co-localized exclusively with Golgi markers (Figure 3F), suggesting a post-Golgi compartment or, at the latest, the apoplastic space as the site for CLEL6 maturation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Golgi-retained constructs are not processed.

claim: Maturation of CLEL9 occurs late in the secretory pathway.
source: Maturation late in the secretory pathway was also observed for CLEL9. Similar to CLEL6, the Δ-KDEL and Δ-XylT constructs for CLEL9 were not processed and were retained in the ER and Golgi, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both CLEL6 and CLEL9 mature after exit from the Golgi, in the TGN, in secretory vesicles, or in the apoplastic space.
source: Our data thus indicate that both CLEL6 and CLEL9 mature after exit from the Golgi, in the TGN, in secretory vesicles, or in the apoplastic space.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization studies showing that processing does not occur in ER or Golgi-retained constructs.

claim: All CLEL peptide precursors including both CLEL6 and 9 share a conserved aspartate upstream of the sulfated tyrosine.
source: All CLEL peptide precursors including both CLEL6 and 9 share a conserved aspartate upstream of the sulfated tyrosine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The aspartate is required for processing of CLEL6 and CLEL9.
source: As compared to the fully processed Δ-Sec constructs of CLEL6 and CLEL9, the larger unprocessed form was observed for the Δ-Sec D71A and Δ-Sec D66A mutants, indicating that the aspartate is indeed required for processing (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: There was no bioactivity in cell wall extracts of plants expressing the alanine-substituted CLEL6 precursor.
source: In contrast, there was no bioactivity in cell wall extracts of plants expressing the alanine-substituted CLEL6 precursor, and reduced bioactivity in extracts from plants expressing the D66A-CLEL9 precursor (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioassay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was reduced bioactivity in extracts from plants expressing the D66A-CLEL9 precursor.
source: In contrast, there was no bioactivity in cell wall extracts of plants expressing the alanine-substituted CLEL6 precursor, and reduced bioactivity in extracts from plants expressing the D66A-CLEL9 precursor (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioassay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The aspartate residue is important for peptide maturation.
source: The data confirm the importance of the aspartate residue for peptide maturation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the processing and bioactivity data for aspartate mutants.

claim: Co-expression of EPI10 reduced the efficiency of processing of Δ-Sec CLEL6 and Δ-Sec CLEL9.
source: As compared to the single, fully processed band that was observed again for Δ-Sec CLEL6 and Δ-Sec CLEL9, co-expression of EPI10 reduced the efficiency of processing resulting in additional bands corresponding to the unprocessed CLEL6 and CLEL9 precursors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Another SBT activity is required, directly or indirectly, for the maturation of CLEL peptides.
source: The data indicate that on top of SBT6.1, another SBT activity is required, directly or indirectly, for the maturation of CLEL peptides.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EPI10 inhibition experiment.

claim: Four SBT genes (SBTs 1.7, 3.7, 3.8, and 4.14) were up-regulated in tpst-1 hypocotyls in comparison to the wild type.
source: We thus analyzed the expression of the 56 Arabidopsis SBT genes in tpst-1 hypocotyls in comparison to the wild type and found that four (SBTs 1.7, 3.7, 3.8, and 4.14) were up-regulated in the tpst-1 background (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SBT3.8 has been described as an aspartate-dependent protease.
source: Interestingly, SBT3.8 (At4g10540) has recently been described as an aspartate-dependent protease, and selectivity for aspartate at the cleavage site was reported to be pH dependent (Chichkova et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Selectivity of SBT3.8 for aspartate at the cleavage site is pH dependent.
source: Interestingly, SBT3.8 (At4g10540) has recently been described as an aspartate-dependent protease, and selectivity for aspartate at the cleavage site was reported to be pH dependent (Chichkova et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: eCLEL6 was processed by SBT3.8 to produce the mature DYPQPHRKPPIHN peptide at pH 5.5.
source: eCLEL6 was processed in a SBT3.8-dependent manner to produce the mature DYPQPHRKPPIHN peptide at pH 5.5 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by MALDI-TOF data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: At pH 7.0, cleavage of eCLEL6 by SBT3.8 was not observed and mature CLEL6 was not produced.
source: In contrast, at pH 7.0, this cleavage was not observed and mature CLEL6 was not produced (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (though not shown in the manuscript).

claim: pH-dependent cleavage of eCLEL6 at acidic pH suggests the trans-Golgi or the cell wall as possible compartments for final processing of the CLEL6 precursor.
source: pH-dependent cleavage of eCLEL6 at acidic pH suggests the trans-Golgi or the cell wall as possible compartments for final processing of the CLEL6 precursor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pH-dependent activity of SBT3.8 and knowledge of pH in different cellular compartments.

claim: SBT3.8 is localized to the apoplastic space in agro-infiltrated tobacco leaves and in stably transformed Arabidopsis lines.
source: Consistent with this proposition, we localized sfGFP-tagged SBT3.8 to the apoplastic space, both in agro-infiltrated tobacco leaves and in stably transformed Arabidopsis lines (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Two cleavage products were observed for the CLEL6 precursor digested with SBT3.8, corresponding to cleavage after D71 and D47.
source: Consistent with the presence of two aspartate residues in the CLEL6 precursor (Figure 2A), two cleavage products were observed (marked by asterisks in Figure 5D), corresponding to cleavage after D71 (upper band) and D47 (lower band).
evidence: This claim is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The upper band corresponding to cleavage after D71 was not observed for the D71A mutant.
source: The upper band was not observed for the D71A mutant, confirming that cleavage at this site is aspartate-dependent (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Cleavage at D71 is aspartate-dependent.
source: The upper band was not observed for the D71A mutant, confirming that cleavage at this site is aspartate-dependent (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the D71A mutation prevents cleavage at this site.

claim: The tyrosine-sulfated CLEL6 precursor was cleaved by SBT3.8 in a time-dependent manner similar to the non-sulfated precursor.
source: The tyrosine-sulfated CLEL6 precursor was cleaved by SBT3.8 in a time-dependent manner similar to the non-sulfated precursor, indicating that tyrosine sulfation does not affect SBT3.8-mediated aspartate-dependent processing (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Tyrosine sulfation does not affect SBT3.8-mediated aspartate-dependent processing.
source: The tyrosine-sulfated CLEL6 precursor was cleaved by SBT3.8 in a time-dependent manner similar to the non-sulfated precursor, indicating that tyrosine sulfation does not affect SBT3.8-mediated aspartate-dependent processing (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that sulfated and non-sulfated precursors are cleaved similarly.

claim: The recombinant CLEL6 precursor was cleaved efficiently by exudates prepared from wild-type plants, but not by sbt3.8 exudates.
source: The recombinant CLEL6 precursor was cleaved efficiently by exudates prepared from wild-type plants, but not by sbt3.8 exudates (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There are other proteases acting redundantly with SBT3.8 in aspartate-dependent CLEL6 maturation.
source: However, we did not observe any defect in the gravitropic response of the hypocotyl in sbt3.8 mutants, suggesting that there are other proteases acting redundantly with SBT3.8 in aspartate-dependent CLEL6 maturation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C; Figure 6).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that sbt3.8 mutants do not show a phenotype despite the in vitro evidence for SBT3.8 activity.

claim: SBTs are required for the gravitropic response of etiolated Arabidopsis seedlings.
source: Using an inhibitor-based approach targeting SBT function at the level of enzyme activity rather than gene expression, we confirmed that SBTs are required for the gravitropic response of etiolated Arabidopsis seedlings (Figure 1A,C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing impaired gravitropism in EPI-expressing plants.

claim: SBT activity is required upstream of the peptides.
source: The loss-of-function phenotype of EPI1a and EPI10-expressing transgenic plants was complemented by application of the mature CLEL6 and CLEL9 peptides (Figure 1B,D), indicating that SBT activity is required upstream of the peptides, consistent with a role in peptide formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complementation experiments.

claim: Cleavage of CLEL precursors by SBT6.1 constitutes the first obligatory processing step in peptide maturation.
source: Cleavage of CLEL precursors by SBT6.1 constitutes the first obligatory processing step in peptide maturation (not considering the co-translational cleavage of the signal peptide).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that SBT6.1 cleavage is required for function.

claim: SBT6.1 cleaves CLEL precursors soon after exit from the ER in an early Golgi compartment.
source: We show here that SBT6.1 cleaves CLEL precursors soon after exit from the ER in an early Golgi compartment (Figure 2), indicating that the reported plasma-membrane localization (Ghorbani et al., 2016) is irrelevant for the maturation of CLEL6 and 9.
evidence: This claim is supported by localization and BFA treatment experiments.

claim: The reported plasma-membrane localization of SBT6.1 is irrelevant for the maturation of CLEL6 and 9.
source: We show here that SBT6.1 cleaves CLEL precursors soon after exit from the ER in an early Golgi compartment (Figure 2), indicating that the reported plasma-membrane localization (Ghorbani et al., 2016) is irrelevant for the maturation of CLEL6 and 9.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that processing occurs in the Golgi.

claim: The variable pro-region of the precursor including the SBT6.1 cleavage sites is important for secretion.
source: The variable pro-region of the precursor including the SBT6.1 cleavage sites is thus important for secretion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutation of SBT6.1 sites impairs secretion.

claim: For brain-derived and glial cell-line derived neurotrophic factors (BDNF and GDNF), the cleavable prodomain was found to be required for post-Golgi trafficking.
source: For brain-derived and glial cell-line derived neurotrophic factors (BDNF and GDNF, respectively) the cleavable prodomain was found to be required for post-Golgi trafficking.
evidence: This is background information from the animal field, supported by established knowledge.

claim: Sorting of BDNF and GDNF to secretory granules depends on sorting receptors of the Vps10p family, sortilin and sorLA, respectively.
source: Sorting of BDNF and GDNF to secretory granules depends on sorting receptors of the Vps10p (vacuolar protein-sorting 10 protein) family, sortilin and sorLA, respectively (Chen et al., 2005; Geng et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Sortilin facilitates prodomain-dependent export of hydrophobic conotoxins from the ER.
source: Sortilin also facilitates prodomain-dependent export of hydrophobic conotoxins from the ER, by allowing them to escape ER quality control mechanisms (Conticello et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The prodomain of CLEL peptides may interact with unidentified sorting receptors to facilitate secretion.
source: Likewise, the prodomain of CLEL peptides may interact with unidentified sorting receptors to facilitate secretion or, alternatively, cleavage of the prodomain by SBT6.1 may provide a point of quality control, before the now partially processed precursor is allowed to leave the Golgi for final activation.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to animal systems.

claim: Cleavage of the prodomain by SBT6.1 may provide a point of quality control before the precursor leaves the Golgi.
source: Likewise, the prodomain of CLEL peptides may interact with unidentified sorting receptors to facilitate secretion or, alternatively, cleavage of the prodomain by SBT6.1 may provide a point of quality control, before the now partially processed precursor is allowed to leave the Golgi for final activation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that SBT6.1 cleavage facilitates secretion.

claim: The requirement of SBT6.1-mediated processing for secretion provides an explanation for why SBT6.1 cleavage sites are required for CLEL6 activity despite not producing the active peptide.
source: The requirement of SBT6.1-mediated processing for secretion provides an explanation for the perplexing finding that SBT6.1 cleavage sites and, by inference, cleavage by SBT6.1 are required for CLEL6 activity (Ghorbani et al., 2016), despite the fact that cleavage at these sites does not produce the active peptide.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the secretion data to previous findings.

claim: Cleavage by SBT6.1 allows for continued passage of partially processed precursors through the secretory pathway, and thereby facilitates subsequent post-translational modifications in the Golgi and post-Golgi compartments.
source: Our data suggest that cleavage by SBT6.1 allows for continued passage of partially processed (pre-activated) precursors through the secretory pathway, and thereby facilitates subsequent post-translational modifications in the Golgi (sulfation, proline hydroxylation) and post-Golgi compartments (proteolytic maturation) (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the secretion and processing data.

claim: The second obligatory processing event and formation of the bioactive peptide hinged on the aspartate residue at the cleavage site.
source: The second obligatory processing event and formation of the bioactive peptide hinged on the aspartate residue at the cleavage site (D71 for CLEL6 and D66 for CLEL9; Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis and bioactivity data.

claim: Cleavage at the N-terminus of CLEL6 and 9 peptides is mediated by Asp-dependent SBT(s).
source: This processing step was inhibited by the SBT-specific inhibitor EPI10 (Tian et al., 2005; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that cleavage at the N-terminus of CLEL6 and 9 peptides also is mediated by SBT(s), particularly by Asp-dependent SBT(s).
evidence: This is an inference based on the EPI10 inhibition experiment.

claim: SBT3.8 is one of the enzymes that ultimately activate CLEL6 and CLEL9.
source: Here, we identified SBT3.8 as one of the enzymes that ultimately activate CLEL6 and CLEL9.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro cleavage assays and expression analysis.

claim: All other members of the plant SBT family except SBT6.1 and 6.2 are secretory enzymes.
source: Unlike SBT6.1 and 6.2, all other members of the plant SBT family are secretory enzymes (Schaller et al., 2018) that co-migrate with potential pro-peptide substrates through the secretory pathway towards the cell wall as their final destination, thus providing ample opportunity for interaction en route.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cleavage of CLEL precursors does not occur before the partially processed precursor leaves the Golgi.
source: Nonetheless, cleavage does not occur before the partially processed precursor leaves the Golgi (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization and processing data shown in Figure 3.

claim: TPST requires aspartate on the amino side of tyrosine for substrate recognition.
source: Interestingly, tyrosin sulfation by TPST is known to depend on an adjacent aspartate residue (Hanai et al., 2000; Komori et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The CLEL6 precursor produced in E. coli was efficiently processed by SBT3.8, despite the lack of tyrosine sulfation.
source: However, this scenario is not supported by our data, since the CLEL6 precursor produced in E. coli was efficiently processed by SBT3.8, despite the lack of tyrosine sulfation.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro cleavage assays.

claim: The sulfated and non-sulfated CLEL6 precursors were found to be cleaved similarly by SBT3.8.
source: In fact, the sulfated und non-sulfated CLEL6 precursors were found to be cleaved similarly by SBT3.8, indicating that tyrosin-sulfation does not affect cleavage site recognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro cleavage assays comparing sulfated and non-sulfated precursors.

claim: Tyrosine-sulfation does not affect cleavage site recognition by SBT3.8.
source: In fact, the sulfated und non-sulfated CLEL6 precursors were found to be cleaved similarly by SBT3.8, indicating that tyrosin-sulfation does not affect cleavage site recognition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that sulfated and non-sulfated precursors are cleaved similarly.

claim: SBT zymogens remain inactive until the prodomain is cleaved off auto-catalytically and subsequently released.
source: SBT zymogens remain inactive until the prodomain is cleaved off auto-catalytically and subsequently released (Anderson et al., 2002; Cedzich et al., 2009; Janzik et al., 2000; Meyer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Prodomain-mediated inhibition and latency of the zymogen are pH-dependent.
source: Prodomain-mediated inhibition and latency of the zymogen are pH-dependent, and broken in a compartment-specific manner as the pH drops along the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protease activation.

claim: For furin, the prodomain is released in a second autocatalytic cleavage event, which does not occur before the zymogen reaches the acidic environment of the TGN.
source: In the well-studied case of furin, for example, the prodomain is released in a second autocatalytic cleavage event, which does not occur before the zymogen reaches the acidic environment of the TGN (Anderson et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: SBT3 from tomato requires the acidic pH of post-Golgi compartments for prodomain cleavage and activation.
source: Similarly, SBT3 from tomato also requires the acidic pH of post-Golgi compartments for prodomain cleavage and activation (Meyer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: pH-dependent release of the inhibitory prodomain may explain why the second obligatory cleavage event by SBT3.8 does not occur before peptide precursors exit the Golgi.
source: These findings may explain why the second obligatory cleavage event by SBT3.8 and, possibly, additional redundant activities does not occur before peptide precursors exit the Golgi.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to other proteases.

claim: Processing of the CLEL6 precursor by SBT3.8 requires an acidic environment which is encountered only after exit from the Golgi.
source: Indeed, we did not observe cleavage of the N-terminally extended eCLEL6 peptide by SBT3.8 at neural pH, whereas mature CLEL6 was produced at pH 5.5 (Figure 5B). We conclude that processing of the CLEL6 precursor by SBT3.8 requires an acidic environment which is encountered only after exit from the Golgi.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pH-dependent activity data and knowledge of cellular pH.

claim: The extracellular localization of SBT3.8 is consistent with precursor processing and release of mature CLEL peptides in post Golgi compartments including the apoplastic space.
source: The extracellular localization of SBT3.8 (Figure 5C) is fully consistent with precursor processing and release of mature CLEL peptides in post Golgi compartments including the apoplastic space.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the localization data to the processing model.
